title: Highly Classified NSA Network Goes Down
description:
"CNN and other outlets are reporting that a classified network at the NSA is down," writes longtime Slashdot reader frdmfghtr. "This follows a week of major outages at Microsoft, the FAA, and JPMorgan Chase." From a report: The network, called NSANet, allows employees to communicate classified information internally. At this point there is no evidence of a cyberattack, sources said. As the agency works to understand the scope of the problem, it has enacted staggered arrivals for personnel, the sources said.
 
"We see no evidence that this was a cyberattack," White House spokesperson Lauren Bis said Tuesday on Newsmax. "There is no crisis, or anything like that, for Americans to be worried about." [...] The US shares intelligence with a group of countries in what is known as the Five Eyes intelligence-sharing alliance, which includes the US, UK, New Zealand, Australia and Canada. That intelligence sharing system has not been impacted as a result of the NSANet outage, according to a source from one of the countries and a former US intelligence official. The NSA released a statement addressing the network issues: "The National Security Agency experienced temporary degradation during scheduled routine maintenance. While some internal systems were affected, mission-critical capabilities remain fully operational and our ability to defend national security continues. NSA's infrastructure is designed with multiple layers of redundancy to maintain operations during planned maintenance or unexpected events."





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: School Phone Bans Are Gradually Improving Test Scores
description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from The New York Times: School cellphone bans are beginning to modestly improve students' academic performance, according to the first large national analysis that compared students' test scores before and after the bans. Schools with strict bans -- requiring students to lock their phones in pouches all school day -- saw math and reading scores improve as if students had an additional week or two of school a year, the study found. It was published Tuesday by the Center for Education Policy Research at Harvard.
 
U.S. students' test scores began falling over a decade ago. The drop coincided with the rise of smartphones, raising questions about their role in the decline. The evidence so far on the academic effects of phone bans has been mixed. But the new study indicates they are starting to have an influence.
 
The study looked at 3.3 million students between 2021 and 2026. They were in third through 10th grade, attending 4,600 U.S. schools. Using scores on MAP tests, which track achievement from fall to spring, it compared the performance of students at schools that put in strict phone bans with those at similar schools that did not have such bans. The annual gains reversed about half the annual loss that an average student experienced in the years leading up to the pandemic. (Students lost even more ground during pandemic closures.) "The earlier studies on cellphone bans have been dismissed as implying small impacts, and in-school cellphone use has been ruled out as playing a big role in the decline," said Thomas Kane, a professor at the Harvard Graduate School of Education and an author of the study. "But we think that's mistaken."





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: Jensen Huang Says He'd Be 'Honored' to Return As Nvidia CEO
description:
In a post on X today, former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang says he would be "honored" to return to the company if its board gives the approval. "I did not live up to the standards expected of everyone at NVIDIA, and I have made serious mistakes in my personal life," he says. "I created problems for the Board that I deeply regret. I own my mistakes completely, and I am committed to cooperating with the Board's independent investigation."
 
Huang resigned from the company last week after acknowledging multiple affairs, including one with a women whom U.S. intelligence officials suspect of being a Chinese spy. NPR reports: His comments come as some in Silicon Valley have tried to argue that Huang was pushed out of the company too quickly, and circulated a petition to "stand with Jensen."
 
"We don't want rushes to judgment. We don't want political pressure from the left or the right to force a board into action before we've even taken the time to turn over the cards and learn what was done," said Brad Gerstner, the founder and CEO of Altimeter Capital, an investor in Nvidia, at Semafor's Silicon Valley and the World conference on Monday. The report notes that Huang and Nvidia's general counsel Tim Teter will answer questions behind closed doors before three congressional committees on December 1 and 2.





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: BugMeNot Calls It Quits
description:
BugMeNot, the password-sharing service launched in 2003 to help users bypass website registration requirements, has shut down without explanation after more than two decades. All that's left on the website is a farewell message that reads: "Thanks to everyone who envisioned a better internet." heise online reports: Founded by Guy King, the service had been online since 2003: BugMeNot was a collection of login credentials for various online services. Volunteers submitted credentials they had created for different websites.
 
The idea was simple: Nobody wants to create a full account and provide all their sensitive information just to use a service occasionally. Two decades ago, this privacy concern was more firmly embedded in the public consciousness, but it has since faded considerably. Back then, usernames and passwords were usually the only access controls, so people could easily submit those credentials. Multifactor authentication was still exotic, and passkeys were a distant prospect.
 
The once-popular service lost its shine after just a few years. Service providers quickly discovered and blocked most of the credentials. They could also prevent users from saving logins for their services directly through BugMeNot, for example when those services were paid. More modern security mechanisms also emerged in recent years. As a result, credentials found on BugMeNot rarely worked. Most online providers also blocked the service's disposable email addresses under @bugmenot.com, making them rarely usable. Many people forgot about the site. Now its operators have shut it down without giving a reason. Additional discussions about BugMeNot's closure can be found on Reddit and Hacker News.





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: Redict deprecated in favor of Valkey
description:
Drew DeVault has
announced that
Redict, a fork of Redis that was created in response to
Redis's 2024 license change, has been deprecated. He recommends switching to Valkey, the permissively licensed Redis fork supported by the Linux Foundation. The two projects are mutually compatible, so switching should be as simple as changing which package is installed and renaming the configuration file.




I had hoped to rally the Redis diaspora around a copyleft initiative, to protect ourselves from future rug-pulls, and made Redict to serve this purpose. However, with the valkey project's success, and Redis's return to a copyleft license, Redict was not able to build a sustainable community.


We recommend that Redict users switch to valkey, which uses a permissive license but has better long-term prospects. We advise against switching back to Redis; though it is once again open source, and copyleft, it uses a contributor license agreement which will facilitate another rug-pull when Redis has a bad financial quarter.

title: Uber Says Hackers Stole Info On Nearly 150K Driver's Licenses During Data Breach
description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from TechCrunch: Uber is notifying close to 150,000 drivers that their personal and driver's license information was stolen during an October data breach at one of the company's tech providers. In notices filed this week with several U.S. attorneys general, including California and Iowa, the ride-hailing giant said it was notified on October 9 by the provider that hackers broke in and stole internal credentials, which were used to access Uber's data.
 
The company said it subsequently began notifying affected drivers that their personal information was stored with the provider. The stolen data includes affected drivers' names, addresses, dates of birth, and driver's license numbers. TechCrunch has learned that the provider is Fireworks AI, which lets developers access and use open-weight AI models. Fireworks reported a data breach last month in which hackers stole its customers' information, including billing data and some private AI datasets.
 
Online productivity startup Notion and AI coding startup Cursor have both confirmed that they had data stolen during the Fireworks hack. In Uber's case, the company said it had alerts enabled to detect unauthorized access to its Fireworks environment, but because the hackers used Fireworks' own internal credentials, "no alerts were triggered." [...] In a notice filed with Oregon's attorney general, Uber said it notified 149,346 people in total that their information had been taken in the breach at Fireworks.





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

provides session management, and so forth; but Zellij also includes a web server for
browser access to a terminal session, is extensible via a plugin API, and is likely
more beginner-friendly than its predecessors. Its most recent release, version 0.46,
adds a standalone terminal emulator, a built-in inbox for notifications, and a settings
screen so users can configure the application without fussing with

yet ready for serious use, it seems stable and full-featured enough to

title: California Sues OpenAI Over Hugging Face, Other AI Model Loss of Control
description:
"California's attorney general just sued OpenAI," writes longtime Slashdot reader destinyland. "The action accuses OpenAI of putting public safety at risk, reports CNBC, specifically by its past failures to contain its AI models within their testing environments." From the report: [California Attorney General Rob Bonta] cited the "infamous" incident in July, where two OpenAI models broke out of a testing environment, gained unauthorized access to the open internet, and breached the internal systems of open-source developer platform Hugging Face. OpenAI said the models were trying to find information that they could use to cheat on an evaluation, and succeeded. The break-in at Hugging Face, which Nvidia acquired for roughly $13 billion in September, rattled industry researchers and prompted government officials to call for more stringent oversight of the AI industry.
 
On Monday, Bonta said that OpenAI later disclosed to his investigators that it was aware of 80 incidents "involving loss of control and access to third-party networks and websites." "But the company failed to provide the detailed information we requested to evaluate these incidents; this is concerning, and it puts the public at risk," he said.
 
Bonta's suit, filed in state Superior Court in San Francisco, alleges OpenAI violated California's Unfair Competition Law and accuses the company of being a public nuisance as defined by state law. The attorney general told reporters he believed in AI's technological power, and the potential of AI models to "achieve scientific breakthroughs, boost economic growth, guard against cyber attacks, and benefit all Californians." "But AI systems must be developed and designed safely," he said. "The companies that develop these models have a moral and yes, a legal responsibility to keep public safety at the forefront." The lawsuit can be found here (PDF).





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: Just 400 US Data Centers Use More Electricity Than Michigan
description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Wired: Just 400 hyperscale data centers connected in the US used as much electricity as the state of Michigan in a single year, new Harvard research has found. The study, published Monday in Nature Sustainability, also finds that the majority of that electricity was generated using fossil fuels, and data center emissions are three times higher than they were before the AI boom. Federal and state governments do not track data center use separate from the rest of the power sector, despite mounting projections that data centers are putting serious strain on the American power grid. Individual data centers' power use is often considered proprietary business information, and data center operators and utilities do not have to disclose specific numbers to the public.
 
The Harvard study specifically focuses on hyperscale data centers -- the largest types of facilities, which have become flashpoints in community opposition across the country. While often used for AI inference or training, not all of the hyperscalers surveyed in this study are being used for AI. [...] To assemble their dataset, the Harvard researchers put together a list of 403 hyperscale data centers around the country that were operational between May 2024 and April 2025 using a mix of industry research and satellite data. The team then modeled these facilities' energy use in a variety of scenarios and calculated the energy mix of the regional grids to estimate individual facilities' carbon emissions. Not all regions were created equal: Data centers in Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa -- the first of which is home to Data Center Alley -- were responsible for more than 50 percent of the energy use in the study. The report notes that these findings may already be outdated. "Some of the massive campuses being proposed today are substantially larger than the typical facility in our dataset," says Gianluca Guidi, a postdoctoral research fellow at Harvard's T. H. Chan School of Public Health and the lead author of the study.
 
The study also excludes onsite power generation, a rapidly growing trend that BloombergNEF estimates could increase overall U.S. emissions by 10% if all proposed projects are built.





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: Comcast's 'Fiber-Powered Wi-Fi' Is Just Cable, AT&T Says In False Advertising Case
description:
AT&T is suing (PDF) Comcast over its "fiber-powered" advertising, arguing that the term misleads consumers into believing Xfinity offers fiber-to-the-home service when most customers actually receive their Internet through coaxial cable. "Comcast should be required to restore to AT&T any and all profits earned as a result of its false and misleading advertising or provide AT&T with any other restitutionary relief the Court deems appropriate," the lawsuit said. The lawsuit asked for a permanent injunction "requiring Comcast to cease describing its hybrid fiber-coaxial service as 'Fiber-Powered.'" Ars Technica reports: While Comcast has deployed plenty of fiber throughout the US, its cable Internet service makes the final connection to homes with coaxial cable. This results in upload speeds being far slower than download speeds. In contrast, fiber-to-the-home service can provide symmetrical upload and download speeds. Comcast has deployed fiber-to-the-home in only small portions of its cable territory while advertising its service as fiber-powered in the majority of areas where cable makes the final connection. AT&T's lawsuit said that in describing its cable broadband as fiber-powered, Comcast "conveys to reasonable consumers the misleading impression that Xfinity Internet is a fiber-to-the-home service comparable to AT&T Fiber. In fact, the vast majority of Xfinity Internet runs over a hybrid fiber-coaxial ('HFC') network, where the critical 'last mile' connection to the customer's home uses copper coaxial cable, not fiber."
 
[...] AT&T previously challenged Comcast's fiber-powered claims through the advertising industry's self-regulatory system operated by BBB National Programs' National Advertising Division (NAD). The NAD determined in June that Comcast accurately described its mix of cable and fiber technology in a disclosure, but that Comcast didn't make the disclosure prominently enough. [...] The NAD recommended that Comcast make the disclosure "more prominent and more proximate to the 'fiber-powered' Wi-Fi claim as necessary to ensure that the disclosure is clear and conspicuous." Comcast said it would comply with the decision, but AT&T's lawsuit makes it clear that it isn't satisfied with the current state of Comcast's advertising. We contacted Comcast and will update this article if it provides a response.





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: FBI Says Artex AI Open-Source Hacking Tool Used to Breach Networks In 'Under Three Hours'
description:
The FBI is warning (PDF) that hackers are using the AI-powered penetration-testing tool Artex to compromise networks in "under three hours" in some cases. The tool has been linked to attacks against South Korean financial institutions, at least 2,250 ConnectWise customers and Barracuda. TechCrunch reports: Artex is one of several open-source AI-powered penetration testing platforms, a category of software built to probe a network's defenses. Hackers can connect Artex to hosted frontier large language models (LLMs) like those from Anthropic and OpenAI, as well as to open-source models and non-U.S. models. The FBI says Artex intrusions can be "noisy," meaning they generate reams of traffic and data that may trigger a targeted company's defensive alerts. But the tools allow hackers to move at speeds that makes it far more harder for human defenders to keep up.
 
In some cases, Artex-linked attacks can move from targeting a system to active compromise "in under three hours." Oftentimes, Artex will rely on rapidly scanning a victim's network to look for signs of weakness, and then exploit simple security bugs, such as weak protections and exposed or stolen passwords to gain a foothold. From there, Artex allows the hacker to spread across the network for databases, mailboxes, and other sensitive information. [...] After Artex was used in cyberattacks, the tool's developer made the software closed-source to prevent further attacks. But the FBI says the previous open-source version continues to circulate and remains "widely accessible" for use in cyberattacks.
 
It's not only companies and targeted victims that have been compromised as a result of weakened security exploited by AI tools; the tools themselves have been exposed as well, potentially allowing outsiders to access powerful hacking capabilities. Last week, researchers found hundreds of publicly exposed Artex systems online, which had been placed on the internet without a password, likely by mistake or misconfiguration -- including the Artex system that was used to target South Korea.





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: Microsoft Outage Leads To Chlorine Gas Poisoning At German Theme Park
description:
Slashdot readers djgl and Mirnotoriety shared a story about how a Microsoft Outlook outage contributed to a chlorine leak at Germany's Phantasialand theme park, injuring 15 guests, four of whom were hospitalized. German broadcasting institution WDR reports (translated to English): We were all affected by this problem: On Friday, there was a disruption that crippled the US software company Microsoft, including its email program Outlook. Phantasialand was also affected. Due to the disruption, no emails were received, as the company informed WDR on Saturday. As a result, no one was aware that the sauna area's maintenance safety system had already issued an email alert. This was because the automatic dosing system had pumped too much chlorine into the pool.
 
Guests at the Hotel Ling Bao in Phantasialand, Bruhl, were injured as a result. They complained of health problems after visiting the pool. The pool was temporarily closed but has since been reopened, as the fire department informed WDR on Saturday. Due to complaints from hotel guests, emergency services and the fire department were called. Thirteen guests complained of respiratory irritation; ultimately, the number of affected individuals rose to a total of 15. Cybersecurity architect and computer scientist Stephan Skrobisch said Microsoft is not responsible for the incident. "It's clearly the system's design that's the problem. They failed to implement an additional notification mechanism."
 
Slashdot reader davidwr agrees, writing in a comment: "Proper alarms would be a hardwired alarm that would be visible or audiable to someone who was on-site who could've gotten everyone out of the water. The blame for the injuries goes to the water park and/or whatever consultant told them it was okay not to have an on-site, hardwired alarm."





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: Apple Eyes 2027 Launch For AI-Powered Smart Glasses
description:
Apple is reportedly targeting WWDC 2027 to unveil its first smart glasses, with shipments planned before the end of that year. According to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman (paywalled), the company has hopes of making them its flagship new product for 2027. Forbes reports: It's no secret that Meta with its Ray-Ban Meta and Oakley Meta glasses, for instance, lead the field when it comes to smart specs. "Apple is counting on integration with the apps people already use on their iPhones to be a key differentiator for the glasses," Gurman said. The App Store has millions of apps while Meta's apps are far fewer. It seems the smart glasses will use a version of the software used on the Vision Pro.
 
"The thinking inside Apple is that while Meta has the increasingly popular Muse agent, Apple has the App Store. Because the Siri integrations are being developed for the iPhone first, software makers won't need to build separate applications for the glasses," Gurman insisted. It seems the glasses will do a lot, from making restaurant reservations to booking cars, ordering coffee or buying movie tickets. "It's also Apple's big AI monetization opportunity," Gurman believes.
 
Part of the experience will depend on Apple's own AI agent system, it seems. There won't be augmented reality in the glasses and they will be lighter than the competition, but with longer battery life and more sensors. Gurman refers to cameras, in the plural, while current models only have one camera, or none at all in the case of Even Realities which tout their privacy aspects. "Apple is also emphasizing the sound quality," Gurman says, "which employees have said is industry-leading, with support for phone calls, music playback and FaceTime audio communication."





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: Corporations Are Using Trump's Tariff Refunds On Bonuses Rather Than Reimbursing
description:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from ProPublica: When Stanley Black & Decker, one of the world's largest tool companies, got hit with President Donald Trump's tariffs last year, the firm made clear that it would be sharing the pain with its customers. The Connecticut-based company raised prices again and again, moves its executives said were necessary because of the new fees on imports. Now, after the Supreme Court struck down Trump's most sweeping tariffs earlier this year, the company is getting at least $298 million refunded. Instead of sharing that bounty with its customers, however, the firm has chosen different recipients: Its own leaders. The company is one of at least nine that have disclosed that they are using their refunds not to pay back the cash-strapped consumers who generally covered much of the tariff costs through higher prices, but to give bonuses, according to a ProPublica analysis of thousands of securities filings and earnings calls for publicly traded companies.
 
Other recognizable companies include the owners of discount department stores TJ Maxx and Marshalls and the golf equipment brand Titleist. Dozens of other firms have said little about how they plan to use the money other than to characterize the windfall as the kind of earnings they use to determine executive bonuses. The Trump administration has not publicly detailed which companies are getting the roughly $170 billion in refunds or how much they've asked for, and it has denied ProPublica's requests for this information. But reporters found some of these details while reviewing the disclosures of thousands of publicly traded companies.
 
Some have described vague plans to pay the money forward by, for example, "returning tariff refunds to our members through pricing," though they generally don't say whether that involves price cuts or limiting future increases. Others are paying back businesses they sold products to because they had itemized receipts that detailed the tariff markups. But consumers hoping for refunds appear to be largely out of luck. With the help of artificial intelligence, ProPublica identified companies that said they planned to refund customers with their tariff windfalls. Almost all of them deal with other businesses, not consumers. "Executive bonuses are probably the least just way to use this money because it wasn't anything the executives did that they should be rewarded for. It was a government mistake that resulted in a refund," said Gregory Germain, a corporate law professor at Syracuse University. "It really explains why it's so important for the government, when they're doing something like this, to think it through to make sure consumers don't pay extra money and not get it back."





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: SpaceX Catches Starship On the First Try
description:
Over the weekend, SpaceX successfully caught a Starship upper stage returning from orbit for the first time, demonstrating a key piece of its plan for a fully and rapidly reusable launch system. The achievement means SpaceX has now demonstrated tower catches of both Starship stages, though not yet on the same flight. "Many small fixes are needed to achieve immediate reusability (like an airplane)," noted SpaceX's Elon Musk. The Register reports: Flight 15 began well, with the 33 Raptor engines of the Super Heavy booster launching the stack from Pad 2 at Starbase, Texas. Hot staging followed, and the booster performed its directional flip maneuver. Thirty-two Raptor engines relit for the boostback burn, intended to return Super Heavy to the tower for another catch. The booster had managed the maneuver on flight tests 5, 7, and 8, but this time something went wrong. "The boostback burn ended early due to low fuel mass," SpaceX said.
 
The booster automatically aborted its return to the tower and diverted offshore. It completed a landing burn, briefly hovering above the Gulf before its engines shut down and the flight termination system delivered an explosive finale. Starship reached orbit under the power of its six Raptor engines and deployed 26 Starlink V3 satellites. Unlike the previous flight's brief orbital stint, this mission lasted almost a day. Following a deorbit burn, Starship returned to the launch site 22 and a half hours after it left.





Read more of this story at Slashdot.

title: [$] A new generation of futexes
description:
Futexes
are a kernel subsystem that provides support for fast mutexes
in user space.  While futexes can indeed be fast, they are not fast enough
for a number of users.  Partly as a result of that, the implementation of
futexes has grown in complexity over the years, with two basic variants
on offer.  The desire for faster futexes remains, though, and that inspires
new patches, including this series
from Suleiman Souhlal adding a third futex class called "futex PING"
for "priority inheritance next generation".
